This appendix provides supplementary resources and support materials to help you succeed in the course.
STAT 579 Final Project: The Target Trial Challenge
Welcome to the capstone experience for STAT 579! This project is where theory becomes practice. You will move beyond textbook exercises to tackle a real-world causal question from start to finish, applying the rigorous principles of modern causal inference to a topic that matters to you.
The challenge? To design and emulate a perfect experiment—a target trial—that you wish had been conducted, using the messy, observational data we so often have in the real world.

The Guiding Philosophy: Think Like a Trialist
At the heart of this project is the Target Trial Emulation framework. Why? Because it provides a powerful and structured way to approach causal inference with observational data.

Imagine you are a detective arriving at a crime scene. You cannot rewind time to see what happened, but you can use the evidence available to reconstruct the most likely sequence of events.
Similarly, we cannot go back in time to run the perfect randomized trial. Instead, we act as “data detectives.” We start by carefully designing the protocol for the ideal experiment we wish we could have run. Then, we use our observational data and causal methods to reconstruct, or emulate, that trial as closely as possible. This disciplined process illuminates our assumptions and strengthens our causal claims.



Your Research Journey: From Question to Conclusion 🗺️
This project will unfold over the semester, with milestones designed to keep you on track. Your journey will follow four key stages:

Formulate a Precise Causal Question (Weeks 1-3): It all starts here. You will identify a compelling causal question and use a DAG to map out your assumptions about the world. What effect do you want to measure? What are the key players (confounders, mediators)?
Design the Ideal Trial (Weeks 4-8): You will write the “protocol” for your hypothetical target trial. Who would be eligible? What are the exact treatment strategies being compared? How would you measure the outcome? This blueprint is your North Star.
Emulate the Trial & Estimate the Effect (Weeks 9-12): This is where you connect your ideal protocol to your chosen dataset. You will apply one or more of the sophisticated methods from our course—like propensity score weighting or g-computation—to estimate the causal effect, carefully checking that your assumptions (like positivity) hold.
Assess Robustness & Interpret (Weeks 13-14): A causal claim is only as strong as its assumptions. You will conduct sensitivity analyses (e.g., calculating an E-value) to see how fragile your results are to potential unmeasured confounding. Finally, you will present your findings and their real-world implications.



Skills You Will Master
By completing this project, you will build and demonstrate a portfolio of in-demand skills:

Causal Reasoning: Translating a real-world problem into a formal causal question with a supporting DAG.
Study Design: Specifying and emulating a target trial protocol.
Modern Estimation: Implementing methods like IPW, matching, or g-computation in R.
Assumption Diagnostics: Assessing positivity, covariate balance, and model fit.
Robustness Checking: Quantifying the potential impact of unmeasured confounding through sensitivity analysis.
Scientific Communication: Presenting your causal findings clearly and honestly in both written and oral formats.



Let’s Get Started
Your first task is the most exciting one: find a question that you are genuinely curious about. Dive into the literature in your field, explore public datasets, or consider a causal puzzle from your own research.

Schedule at a Glance

Week 1 — Instructor demo (no submissions)
Week 2 — DAGs & Assumption Transparency Pearl (1995) Biometrika. Focus: d‑separation, backdoor sets, DAG as data‑generating story.
Week 3 — Exchangeability, Positivity, Consistency Rubin (1974) JEP. Focus: \(Y^1,Y^0\), SUTVA, exchangeability vs. design.
Week 4 — Confounding, Selection, Measurement Bias Hernán, Hernández‑Díaz, & Robins (2004) Epidemiology. Focus: collider/selection bias, loss to follow‑up as conditioning.
Week 5 — Propensity Scores Rosenbaum & Rubin (1983) Biometrika. Focus: balancing score, overlap, matching/stratification/weighting.
Week 6 — IPTW, MSMs, DR Robins, Hernán, & Brumback (2000) Epidemiology. Focus: time‑varying confounding, stabilized weights, pseudo‑populations.
Week 7 — G‑computation Snowden, Rose, & Mortimer (2011) AJE. Focus: standardization via outcome modeling vs. IPTW.
Week 8 — Instrumental Variables Angrist, Imbens, & Rubin (1996) JASA. Focus: IV assumptions, LATE, monotonicity, principal strata.
Week 9 — Effect Modification Yusuf et al. (1991) JAMA. Focus: pre‑specification, multiplicity, tests of interaction.
Week 10 — Mediation I (Foundations) Pearl (2014) Psychological Methods. Focus: CDE vs. NDE/NIE, mediation formulae and assumptions.
Week 11 — Mediation II & Principal Stratification Imai, Keele, & Tingley (2010) Psychological Methods. Focus: sequential ignorability, software, sensitivity.
Week 12 — Sensitivity Analysis VanderWeele & Ding (2017) Ann Intern Med. Focus: E‑value interpretation/limits.
Week 13 — Target Trial Emulation Hernán & Robins (2016) AJE. Focus: 7 components, time zero, immortal time, assignment procedure.



Critique Deliverables & Deadlines

What to submit each week (Weeks 2–13):

2‑page critique (max 900 words, not counting figures/refs)
One-page DAG with minimal sufficient adjustment set(s) highlighted
Assumption log (bullet list) + robustness plan (≤10 bullets)
Reproducible appendix (R code or pseudocode) for at least one key diagnostic (balance, overlap, weight diagnostics, or a small sensitivity calc)

When: Mondays 11:59 pm MT (the night before our Tue class)
Where: Canvas → “Weekly Paper Critique — Week X”
Collaboration: Discuss ideas freely; write/code your own submission.



How to Write a Great Critique
Use our Assumption‑Centric 4‑Step:

Study Design → Causal Question

State the estimand (e.g., \(ATE\), \(ATT\), \(LATE\), NDE/NIE).
Write the target trial version in one paragraph (eligibility, treatment strategies, time zero, outcome, follow‑up, causal contrast).

Method Selection → Identification

Draw the DAG; list minimal backdoor sets (if applicable).
If IV/mediation/MSM, write assumptions explicitly (relevance, independence, exclusion; sequential ignorability; positivity; consistency; no interference).
Note any positivity risks (sparse cells/extreme propensities).

Assumption Validation → Diagnostics

Exchangeability: covariate balance & overlap plots; placebo/negative controls (if available).
Positivity: common support figures, weight distribution summaries (mean/sd/skew, max).
Modeling: mis‑specification checks, flexible learners where helpful.
Sensitivity: E‑values; IV falsification tests; Rosenbaum bounds; alternative specs.

Interpretation → Uncertainty Communication

Interpret the causal estimand with audience‑appropriate language; flag scope (population, time).
State where violations would flip conclusions.
Offer at least one alternative method that could triangulate the main claim.




Templates & Checklists

A) 2‑Page Critique Template (copy/paste)

Title: Week X — [Paper Title] — STAT 579 Critique
Causal Question & Estimand (≤120 words): …
Target Trial (≤120 words): Eligibility; treatment strategies; time zero; outcome; follow‑up; causal contrast.
DAG (figure): include nodes and arrows; highlight chosen adjustment set.
Identification Plan (≤150 words): backdoor/IV/mediation/MSM rationale.
Diagnostics (bullets): balance/overlap; weight quality; model checks.
Sensitivity (bullets): E‑value or alternative; what violation would overturn results.
Interpretation (≤120 words): estimand in plain language; limitations; - generalizability.
Repro Appendix: code or pseudocode for one diagnostic.



B) DAG Checklist (quick yes/no)

All pre‑treatment common causes included?
No conditioning on colliders or their descendants?
If time‑varying confounders exist, did you avoid “adjusting them away” in outcome models (favor MSM/IPTW)?
Is the minimal sufficient set clearly highlighted?
Are measurement error nodes (if suspected) represented?



C) Positivity & Weight Quality

Report: % with \(\hat e(X)\in[0.1,0.9]\); histogram/density; stabilized weight mean≈1, sd small, max reasonable (<10 suggested for weekly demos).
If violations: restrict support, coarsen covariates, or switch method (e.g., g‑comp/TMLE).



D) Sensitivity Menu (pick ≥1)

E‑value for point & CI limit
Rosenbaum bounds (binary outcomes)
Placebo/negative control (if plausible)
IV falsification (balance on observables; over‑id tests with caution)
Sequential ignorability stress tests (mediation)




Starter R Snippets
Propensity, Overlap, and Balance
library(WeightIt); library(cobalt)
w <- weightit(A ~ X1+X2+X3, data=df, method="ps", estimand="ATE")
love.plot(bal.tab(w), thresholds=c(m=.1))
summary(w$weights)  # check mean≈1 (if stabilized), max, skew
IPTW for MSM (stabilized)
num <- glm(A ~ L0, family=binomial, data=df)      # numerator model (coarse)
den <- glm(A ~ L0+L1, family=binomial, data=df)   # denominator model
sw  <- predict(num, type="response")/predict(den, type="response")
msm <- glm(Y ~ A, weights=sw, data=df)            # simple MSM
G‑computation (parametric)
mY <- glm(Y ~ A + X1 + X2, family=gaussian, data=df)
mu1 <- mean(predict(mY, newdata=transform(df, A=1), type="response"))
mu0 <- mean(predict(mY, newdata=transform(df, A=0), type="response"))
ATE <- mu1 - mu0
Mediation (NDE/NIE via mediation)
library(mediation)
mM <- glm(M ~ A + X, family=binomial, data=df)
mY <- glm(Y ~ A + M + X, family=binomial, data=df)
med <- mediate(mM, mY, treat="A", mediator="M", sims=1000)
summary(med)  # NDE/NIE under sequential ignorability
E‑value (risk ratio)
library(EValue)
evalue.RR(est=2.5, lo=1.8, hi=3.4)

title: Causal Inference Notation Guide
text:
A well-defined preamble is key for efficiency. These macros provide shortcuts for commonly used mathematical notation.
% --- Core Symbols & Operators ---
\newcommand{\PP}{\mathbb{P}} % probability
\newcommand{\E}[1]{\mathbb{E}\left[#1\right]} % Expectation
\newcommand{\Es}[2]{\mathbb{E}_{#1}\left[#2\right]} % Expectation with subscript
\newcommand{\Prob}[1]{\mathbb{P}\left(#1\right)} % Probability with parentheses
\newcommand{\var}[1]{\operatorname{Var}\left[#1\right]}
\newcommand{\cov}[2]{\operatorname{Cov}\left(#1, #2\right)}
\newcommand{\indep}{\perp\!\!\!\perp} % Independence symbol
\newcommand{\doop}[1]{\operatorname{do}\left(#1\right)} % do-operator
\newcommand{\ind}[1]{\mathbb{I}\left\{#1\right\}}   % Indicator function

% --- Mathematical Sets & Vectors ---
\newcommand{\RR}{\mathbb{R}} % Real numbers
\newcommand{\NN}{\mathbb{N}} % Natural numbers
\newcommand{\vect}[1]{\mathbf{#1}} % Vector notation



At the heart of any causal analysis are key variables. It’s crucial to distinguish between a random variable and a fixed value. The support of a random variable is the set of all possible values it can take.









Symbol
Type
Support (\(\mathcal{A}\), \(\mathcal{Y}\), etc.)
Description & Interpretation




\(i\)
Fixed Index
\({1, \dots, n}\)
A single unit or individual in a sample of size \(n\)


\(A, A_i\)
Random Variable
\(\mathcal{A}\), typically \({0, 1}\)
Treatment/Exposure. The value of \(A_i\) is not known until it is observed


\(a\)
Fixed Value
\(a \in \mathcal{A}\)
A specific, hypothetical level of treatment (e.g., \(a=1\))


\(Y, Y_i\)
Random Variable
\(\mathcal{Y} \subseteq \mathbb{R}\)
Outcome. The variable we want to affect


\(y\)
Fixed Value
\(y \in \mathcal{Y}\)
A specific, hypothetical outcome value


\(X, X_i\)
Random Variable
\(\mathcal{X} \subseteq \RR\)
Covariates. A variable of baseline characteristics (e.g., age) that may affect treatment assignment or the outcome


\(\vect{X}, \vect{X}_i\)
Random Vector
\(\mathcal{X} \subseteq \RR^d\)
A vector of baseline covariates. Bold X signifies a collection of multiple variables (e.g., age, sex, baseline health)


\(Z, Z_i\)
Random Variable
\(\mathcal{Z}\), typically \({0, 1}\)
An Instrumental Variable (IV)


\(M, M_i\)
Random Variable
\(\mathcal{M} \subseteq \RR\)
A Mediator. A post-treatment variable on the causal pathway


\(C\), \(C_i\)
Explicit confounder variable
\(\mathcal{C} \subseteq \RR\)
Variable explicitly used to distinguish from general covariates


\(\vect{C}\)
Vector of confounders
\(\mathcal{C} \subseteq \RR^d\)
Vector of explicit confounding variables


\(L\), \(L_i\)
Time-indexed confounder
\(\mathcal{L} \subseteq \RR\)
Time-indexed or longitudinal confounder (in MSM contexts)


\(\vect{L}\)
Vector of confounders
\(\mathcal{L} \subseteq \RR^d\)
Vector of time-indexed or longitudinal confounders (in MSM contexts)






This framework forces us to think about counterfactual worlds to define causal effects.









Notation
How to Read It
Random vs. Fixed
Interpretation




\(Y_i^a\)
“The potential outcome Y for individual i under treatment a.”
\(Y_i^a\) is a random variable. The superscript a is a fixed value.
This represents the outcome that would have been observed for person i if their treatment had been set to level a.


\(A_i^z\)
“The potential treatment A for individual i under instrument z.”
\(A_i^z\) is a random variable. The superscript z is a fixed value.
This is the treatment person i would have if their instrument Z were set to z.


\(Y^{a, M^{a'}}\)
“Y under treatment a and the mediator value that would have occurred under treatment a'.”
\(Y^{a, M^{a'}}\) is a random variable. Superscripts a and a' are fixed. \(M^{a'}\) is a random variable.
A nested counterfactual for mediation. It asks: what would Y be if we set A to a but forced M to the value it would have naturally taken if A had been a'?






No causal conclusion is possible without untestable assumptions. Being explicit about them is paramount.








Assumption
Notation / Name
Explanation




Consistency
If \(A_i = a\), then \(Y_i = Y_i^a\).
The observed outcome for an individual is their potential outcome corresponding to the treatment they actually received. This links the observed data to the counterfactual world.


SUTVA
Stable Unit Treatment Value Assumption
Two parts: (1) No interference: My treatment doesn’t affect your outcome. (2) One version of treatment: The effect of the treatment is the same for everyone who receives it.


Exchangeability
\(Y^a \indep A\)
The potential outcomes are independent of the treatment that was actually assigned. This is the “as if random” assumption that holds in an ideal RCT.


Conditional Exchangeability
\(Y^a \indep A \mid \vect{X}\)
Within levels of the covariates \(\vect{X}\), treatment assignment is random. This is the key assumption for observational studies, also called ignorability or no unmeasured confounding.


Positivity
\(0 < \Prob{A=a \mid \vect{X}=\vect{x}} < 1\)
For every group of individuals with the same covariate values \(\vect{x}\), some received treatment and some did not. There are no groups with a 0% or 100% chance of treatment.






DAGs are visual representations of our causal assumptions, providing a powerful way to assess confounding. A DAG consists of nodes (variables) and directed edges (arrows) representing causal effects.








Concept
Description
Example




Path
A sequence of connected nodes. Can go along or against arrows.
\(A \to M \to Y\) is a causal path. \(A \leftarrow X \to Y\) is a non-causal path.


Confounder
A common cause of \(A\) and \(Y\).
A variable \(X\) with paths \(X \to A\) and \(X \to Y\). This creates a “backdoor” path.


Mediator
A variable \(M\) on the causal pathway from \(A\) to \(Y\).
A variable \(M\) in the path \(A \to M \to Y\).


Collider
A common effect of two other variables.
A variable \(C\) in a path like \(A \to C \leftarrow Y\). Conditioning on a collider opens a non-causal path and induces bias.


d-separation
A graphical rule for determining if variables are independent. Two variables are d-separated if all paths between them are blocked. A path is blocked if it contains a non-collider that is conditioned on, or a collider that is not conditioned on.







The do-operator: \(\E{Y \mid \doop{A=a}}\) represents the expectation of \(Y\) in a hypothetical world where we intervene and set A=a for everyone. This is mathematically equivalent to the potential outcome expectation \(\E{Y^a}\).
Backdoor Criterion: The causal effect of \(A\) on \(Y\) is identified if we can find a set of covariates \(\vect{X}\) that blocks all non-causal (“backdoor”) paths from \(A\) to \(Y\). If \(\vect{X}\) satisfies this, then:

\[
\E{Y^a} = \sum_{\vect{x}} \E{Y \mid A=a, \vect{X}=\vect{x}} \Prob{\vect{X}=\vect{x}}
\]




Mediation analysis decomposes the total effect of \(A\) on \(Y\) into a direct effect and an indirect effect that travels through a mediator \(M\).



Natural Direct Effect (NDE): The effect of changing treatment from 0 to 1 while forcing the mediator to stay at the level it would have naturally taken under no treatment.

\[
\text{NDE} = \E{Y^{a=1, M^{a=0}} - Y^{a=0, M^{a=0}}}
\]

Natural Indirect Effect (NIE): The effect of holding treatment fixed at 1, but changing the mediator from its natural level under control to its natural level under treatment.

\[
\text{NIE} = \E{Y^{a=1, M^{a=1}} - Y^{a=1, M^{a=0}}}
\]

Total Effect (TE): \(\text{TE} = \text{NDE} + \text{NIE} = \E{Y^1 - Y^0}\)




To identify the NDE and NIE, we need four conditional exchangeability assumptions (no unmeasured confounding) for the following relationships, conditional on baseline covariates \(\vect{X}\):

The effect of treatment \(A\) on the outcome \(Y\).
The effect of treatment \(A\) on the mediator \(M\).
The effect of the mediator \(M\) on the outcome \(Y\).
There is no confounder of the \(M-Y\) relationship that is itself affected by the treatment \(A\).








Goal: Estimate \(\E{Y^a}\) by modeling the outcome.
Formula: \[
\E{Y^a} = \sum_x \E{Y \mid A=a, \vect{X}= \vect{x}} \Prob{\vect{X}= \vect{x}} = \Es{\vect{X}}{\E{Y \mid A=a, \vect{X}=\vect{x}}}
\]





Goal: Create a “pseudo-population” where treatment assignment is independent of \(\vect{X}\).
Propensity Score: The probability of receiving treatment: \(e(\vect{X}) = \Prob{A=1 \mid \vect{X}}\).
IP Weight (for ATE): The weight for each individual i is the inverse of their probability of receiving the treatment they actually got:

\[
w_i = \frac{A_i}{e(\vect{X}_i)} + \frac{1-A_i}{1-e(\vect{X}_i)}
\]

ATE Estimator:

\[
\hat{\E{Y^a}} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \frac{\ind{A_{i}=a}Y_{i}}{\Prob{A_{i}=a \mid \vect{X}_{i}}}
\]




While the parenthesis notation \(Y(a, M(a'))\) is arguably more explicit, the superscript notation \(Y^{a, M^{a'}}\) is also widely used, particularly in the tradition of Pearl’s work. The key is to be very precise in our interpretation.
Here is the revised section using the superscript notation, with a detailed breakdown to ensure clarity.


The nested potential outcome notation used in mediation, \(Y^{a, M^{a'}}\), is powerful and compact, but it requires careful interpretation to distinguish between direct interventions and natural counterfactual values.
Let’s break it down to fully understand its meaning. Think of the superscript as having two distinct components that describe a complex hypothetical world.

The First Component: A Direct Intervention on \(A\)

The \(a\) in the superscript represents a direct intervention. We are imagining a world where we actively set the treatment \(A\) to the fixed value \(a\).

The Second Component: A Counterfactual Value for \(M\)

The \(M^{a'}\) part is more subtle. This does not mean we are intervening on \(M\). Instead, \(M^{a'}\) represents the potential value of the mediator.
How to Read \(M^{a'}\): “The value that the mediator \(M\) would have naturally taken if treatment \(A\) had been set to \(a'\).” This is a random variable, representing a natural outcome under a hypothetical condition.




The full expression combines these two ideas:

“The potential outcome \(Y\) that would be realized if we intervened to set treatment \(A\) to \(a\), while the mediator \(M\) simultaneously took on the value it would have naturally had if treatment had been set to \(a'\).”

This notation describes a complex counterfactual scenario where one variable (\(A\)) is set by intervention, while another variable (\(M\)) is determined by a separate counterfactual condition.



This detailed interpretation makes the definitions of the direct and indirect effects clear.

Natural Direct Effect (NDE)

Formula: \(\text{NDE} = \E{Y^{a=1, M^{a=0}} - Y^{a=0, M^{a=0}}}\)
Interpretation: We compare two hypothetical worlds. In both, the mediator is held to the value it would have naturally taken under the control condition (\(M^{a=0}\)). The only difference is our direct intervention on \(A\), changing it from 0 to 1. Any resulting change in the average outcome is therefore the direct effect of \(A\) that does not pass through \(M\).

Natural Indirect Effect (NIE)

Formula: \(\text{NIE} = \E{Y^{a=1, M^{a=1}} - Y^{a=1, M^{a=0}}}\)
Interpretation: Here, our direct intervention on \(A\) is held constant at the treated level (\(a=1\)) in both scenarios. The only thing we change is the mediator’s value—from the natural level it would have under control (\(M^{a=0}\)) to the natural level it would have under treatment (\(M^{a=1}\)). Any change in the average outcome must be due to the causal pathway that is transmitted through the mediator.

section: STAT 579 Final Project: The Target Trial Challenge
text:
STAT 579 Final Project: The Target Trial Challenge
Welcome to the capstone experience for STAT 579! This project is where theory becomes practice. You will move beyond textbook exercises to tackle a real-world causal question from start to finish, applying the rigorous principles of modern causal inference to a topic that matters to you.
The challenge? To design and emulate a perfect experiment—a target trial—that you wish had been conducted, using the messy, observational data we so often have in the real world.

The Guiding Philosophy: Think Like a Trialist
At the heart of this project is the Target Trial Emulation framework. Why? Because it provides a powerful and structured way to approach causal inference with observational data.

Imagine you are a detective arriving at a crime scene. You cannot rewind time to see what happened, but you can use the evidence available to reconstruct the most likely sequence of events.
Similarly, we cannot go back in time to run the perfect randomized trial. Instead, we act as “data detectives.” We start by carefully designing the protocol for the ideal experiment we wish we could have run. Then, we use our observational data and causal methods to reconstruct, or emulate, that trial as closely as possible. This disciplined process illuminates our assumptions and strengthens our causal claims.



Your Research Journey: From Question to Conclusion 🗺️
This project will unfold over the semester, with milestones designed to keep you on track. Your journey will follow four key stages:

Formulate a Precise Causal Question (Weeks 1-3): It all starts here. You will identify a compelling causal question and use a DAG to map out your assumptions about the world. What effect do you want to measure? What are the key players (confounders, mediators)?
Design the Ideal Trial (Weeks 4-8): You will write the “protocol” for your hypothetical target trial. Who would be eligible? What are the exact treatment strategies being compared? How would you measure the outcome? This blueprint is your North Star.
Emulate the Trial & Estimate the Effect (Weeks 9-12): This is where you connect your ideal protocol to your chosen dataset. You will apply one or more of the sophisticated methods from our course—like propensity score weighting or g-computation—to estimate the causal effect, carefully checking that your assumptions (like positivity) hold.
Assess Robustness & Interpret (Weeks 13-14): A causal claim is only as strong as its assumptions. You will conduct sensitivity analyses (e.g., calculating an E-value) to see how fragile your results are to potential unmeasured confounding. Finally, you will present your findings and their real-world implications.



Skills You Will Master
By completing this project, you will build and demonstrate a portfolio of in-demand skills:

Causal Reasoning: Translating a real-world problem into a formal causal question with a supporting DAG.
Study Design: Specifying and emulating a target trial protocol.
Modern Estimation: Implementing methods like IPW, matching, or g-computation in R.
Assumption Diagnostics: Assessing positivity, covariate balance, and model fit.
Robustness Checking: Quantifying the potential impact of unmeasured confounding through sensitivity analysis.
Scientific Communication: Presenting your causal findings clearly and honestly in both written and oral formats.



Let’s Get Started
Your first task is the most exciting one: find a question that you are genuinely curious about. Dive into the literature in your field, explore public datasets, or consider a causal puzzle from your own research.

section: How to Write a Great Critique
text:
How to Write a Great Critique
Use our Assumption‑Centric 4‑Step:

Study Design → Causal Question

State the estimand (e.g., \(ATE\), \(ATT\), \(LATE\), NDE/NIE).
Write the target trial version in one paragraph (eligibility, treatment strategies, time zero, outcome, follow‑up, causal contrast).

Method Selection → Identification

Draw the DAG; list minimal backdoor sets (if applicable).
If IV/mediation/MSM, write assumptions explicitly (relevance, independence, exclusion; sequential ignorability; positivity; consistency; no interference).
Note any positivity risks (sparse cells/extreme propensities).

Assumption Validation → Diagnostics

Exchangeability: covariate balance & overlap plots; placebo/negative controls (if available).
Positivity: common support figures, weight distribution summaries (mean/sd/skew, max).
Modeling: mis‑specification checks, flexible learners where helpful.
Sensitivity: E‑values; IV falsification tests; Rosenbaum bounds; alternative specs.

Interpretation → Uncertainty Communication

Interpret the causal estimand with audience‑appropriate language; flag scope (population, time).
State where violations would flip conclusions.
Offer at least one alternative method that could triangulate the main claim.

Starter R Snippets
Propensity, Overlap, and Balance
library(WeightIt); library(cobalt)
w <- weightit(A ~ X1+X2+X3, data=df, method="ps", estimand="ATE")
love.plot(bal.tab(w), thresholds=c(m=.1))
summary(w$weights)  # check mean≈1 (if stabilized), max, skew
IPTW for MSM (stabilized)
num <- glm(A ~ L0, family=binomial, data=df)      # numerator model (coarse)
den <- glm(A ~ L0+L1, family=binomial, data=df)   # denominator model
sw  <- predict(num, type="response")/predict(den, type="response")
msm <- glm(Y ~ A, weights=sw, data=df)            # simple MSM
G‑computation (parametric)
mY <- glm(Y ~ A + X1 + X2, family=gaussian, data=df)
mu1 <- mean(predict(mY, newdata=transform(df, A=1), type="response"))
mu0 <- mean(predict(mY, newdata=transform(df, A=0), type="response"))
ATE <- mu1 - mu0
Mediation (NDE/NIE via mediation)
library(mediation)
mM <- glm(M ~ A + X, family=binomial, data=df)
mY <- glm(Y ~ A + M + X, family=binomial, data=df)
med <- mediate(mM, mY, treat="A", mediator="M", sims=1000)
summary(med)  # NDE/NIE under sequential ignorability
E‑value (risk ratio)
library(EValue)
evalue.RR(est=2.5, lo=1.8, hi=3.4)

title: Exchangeability & Positivity
text:
Welcome, students, to the third week of Applied Causal Inference. This week marks a pivotal transition in our course. We are moving from the controlled, idealized environment of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) into the messy, complex world of observational data. In the real world, we can’t force people into treatment or control groups; they select themselves, and this selection process is rarely random.
Our central challenge is this: How can we make fair, apples-to-apples comparisons when the groups we want to compare started out as apples and oranges?
The answer lies in understanding and satisfying two foundational assumptions that form the bedrock of causal inference with observational data: exchangeability and positivity. 🧠 These concepts allow us to statistically emulate an RCT, creating a situation of “as-if randomness.” We will spend this week defining these assumptions, exploring their profound implications, and learning how to use powerful graphical tools—Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs)—to help us meet them. Mastering these ideas is not just a theoretical exercise; it is the absolute prerequisite for any credible causal claim you will make in your future research.

title: Exchangeability & Positivity
text:
Learning Objectives
By the end of this module, you will be able to:

Define and Differentiate: Clearly articulate the difference between unconditional exchangeability (the gift of randomization) and conditional exchangeability (the goal of observational analysis) using formal potential outcomes notation.
Explain the ‘Why’: Explain in plain language why conditional exchangeability and positivity are the core, indispensable assumptions for identifying causal effects from non-randomized data.
Translate and Model: Translate your scientific knowledge and assumptions about a real-world problem into the formal language of a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG).
Identify and Justify: Apply the backdoor criterion to a given DAG to identify a sufficient adjustment set of covariates and rigorously justify why this set allows for causal effect estimation.
Diagnose and Act: Use graphical and statistical tools in R to diagnose potential violations of the positivity (overlap) assumption and propose appropriate analytical actions.
Distinguish with Precision: Articulate the crucial conceptual distinction between identification—the theoretical possibility of answering a causal question under ideal assumptions—and estimation—the statistical process of calculating a numerical answer from finite, messy data.

title: Exchangeability & Positivity
text:
1. Comprehensive Topic Explanation
Our journey begins with the fundamental problem of causal inference: we can only ever observe one potential outcome for any given individual. We see the outcome under the treatment they received, but the outcome under the treatment they didn’t receive remains forever in a parallel universe. To bridge this gap and estimate average causal effects, we need a way to make the groups we are comparing… well, comparable.

From Unconditional to Conditional Exchangeability: The Core Idea
Let’s formalize our key concepts. Let \(A\) be a binary treatment, \(Y\) be the observed outcome, and \(Y^a\) be the potential outcome an individual would have experienced had they received treatment level \(a\).
Unconditional Exchangeability: The “Gold Standard” of RCTs
In a perfectly executed RCT, randomization ensures that the treatment and control groups are identical on average across all baseline characteristics—measured and unmeasured. This property is unconditional exchangeability.
Mathematically, we write this as:
\[
Y^a \indep A \quad \text{for all } a
\]

In Plain English: This formula says an individual’s potential outcomes (\(Y^a\)) are statistically independent (\(\indep\)) of the treatment they actually received (\(A\)). Knowing which group a person was randomized to gives you no information about how they would have fared under either treatment option.

When this holds, the observed association is a pure measure of causation:
\[
\underbrace{\E{Y \mid A=1} - \E{Y \mid A=0}}_{\text{Observed Association}} = \underbrace{\E{Y^1} - \E{Y^0}}_{\text{Average Causal Effect (ATE)}}
\]
This is why RCTs are the gold standard. They give us exchangeability for free.
Conditional Exchangeability: Our Goal in Observational Studies
In observational studies, we must concede that the groups are different. Our hope is to achieve conditional exchangeability. We assume the groups are comparable after we account for, or condition on, a set of relevant covariates, which we will denote as a vector \(\vect{L}\). This is the famous “no unmeasured confounding” assumption.
Mathematically, we write this as:
\[
Y^a \indep A \mid \vect{L} \quad \text{for all } a
\]

In Plain English: This says that within any specific stratum defined by the covariates in \(\vect{L}\) (e.g., among 65-year-old female non-smokers), the reason a person received the treatment is unrelated to their potential outcome. For people who are identical on \(\vect{L}\), treatment assignment is “as good as random.”

If this critical assumption holds, we can identify the causal effect via adjustment. A common form is standardization (the g-formula), where we calculate the effect within each stratum of \(\vect{L}\) and then average those effects up to the full population level (Hernán & Robins, 2020, Chapter 2).


The Backdoor Criterion: A GPS for Confounding
The assumption of “no unmeasured confounding” begs the question: which variables must be in our set \(\vect{L}\)? Conditioning on the wrong variables can be worse than conditioning on nothing at all.
This is where Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs) and Judea Pearl’s backdoor criterion provide a rigorous, graphical roadmap (Pearl2016-jc?).
A backdoor path is a non-causal pathway between treatment \(A\) and outcome \(Y\). It’s a source of confounding that creates a spurious association.






The Backdoor Criterion 🗺️



A set of variables \(\vect{L}\) satisfies the backdoor criterion (and is thus a sufficient adjustment set) if two conditions are met:

No node in \(\vect{L}\) is a descendant of the treatment \(A\).
\(\vect{L}\) blocks every backdoor path between \(A\) and \(Y\).



If you find a set \(\vect{L}\) that meets these conditions, adjusting for \(\vect{L}\) is sufficient to achieve conditional exchangeability. The causal effect is then identified by the adjustment formula:
\[
\E{Y^a} = \sum_{\vect{l}} \E{Y \mid A=a, \vect{L}=\vect{l}} \Prob{\vect{L}=\vect{l}}
\]

In Plain English: This formula describes a three-step process:

Stratify: Go into each specific subgroup defined by the values of \(\vect{L}=\vect{l}\).
Compare: Within that subgroup, calculate the average outcome among the treated (\(\E{Y \mid A=a, \vect{L}=\vect{l}}\)).
Average: Calculate a weighted average of these subgroup-specific means, where the weights are the prevalence of each subgroup (\(\Prob{\vect{L}=\vect{l}}\)) in the total population.




Positivity: The Assumption of Common Support
There is one final, crucial assumption: positivity, also known as overlap or common support.






The Positivity Assumption



For every combination of covariates \(\vect{L}=\vect{l}\) that exists in your population, the probability of receiving any given level of treatment must be greater than zero.
\[
0 < \Prob{A=a \mid \vect{L}=\vect{l}} < 1 \quad \text{for all } \vect{l} \text{ such that } \Prob{\vect{L}=\vect{l}} \neq 0
\]



In Plain English: Positivity means that for any “type” of person in your study (defined by their covariates \(\vect{L}\)), there is at least some chance they could have received the treatment and at least some chance they could have received the control.
Why it’s essential: If positivity is violated, it means we have certain subgroups for whom we can’t make a comparison because everyone in that subgroup received the same treatment. We lack the necessary “common support” to make a valid comparison and would be forced to extrapolate.

title: Exchangeability & Positivity
text:
2. Intuitive Clarifications of Challenging Ideas

Analogy 1: The Confounding Coffee Shop ☕
Imagine you want to know the causal effect of drinking espresso (\(A\)) on productivity (\(Y\)). You observe that espresso drinkers are more productive. But is this causal?

The Backdoor Path: You learn that your office has two types of employees: engineers and marketers (our confounder, \(L\)). Engineers are naturally more productive in the morning and they also happen to love espresso.
The DAG: \(L \to A\) and \(L \to Y\). This creates a backdoor path: \(A \leftarrow L \rightarrow Y\). “Being an engineer” is a common cause of both treatment and outcome.
Blocking the Path: To find the true effect of espresso, you must block this backdoor path by adjusting for job type (\(L\)). You achieve this by comparing engineers who drink espresso to other engineers who don’t, and so on. By making comparisons within strata of \(L\), you have controlled for the confounding.



Analogy 2: The Positivity Parachute Problem 🪂
Let’s test the causal effect of using a parachute (\(A\)) on survival (\(Y\)).

The Covariate (\(\vect{L}\)): Let’s define a single covariate: \(L=1\) if “jumping from a plane at 10,000 feet” and \(L=0\) if “standing on the ground.”
The Positivity Violation: Consider the subgroup of people where \(L=1\). In this group, what is the probability of being in the control group (\(A=0\), no parachute)? It’s zero. \(\Prob{A=0 \mid L=1} = 0\).
The Consequence: Because there is no one in the control group for the “jumping from a plane” stratum, we have no data on the counterfactual. We cannot make a comparison. We have a complete lack of overlap.

title: Exchangeability & Positivity
text:
3. Simple, Hand-Calculation Numerical Example(s)
Let’s investigate if a new heart medication (\(A\)) reduces 1-year mortality (\(Y=1\)). We suspect that physicians are more likely to prescribe it to sicker patients. Our confounder is disease “Severity” (\(L\)).
Observed Data (N=410):




Medicated (A=1)
Not Medicated (A=0)
Total




Died (Y=1)
70
30
100


Survived (Y=0)
130
180
310


Total
200
210
410



Step 1: Calculate the Crude (and Misleading) Association The crude risk difference is:
\[
\text{Risk Diff}_{\text{crude}} = \Prob{Y=1 \mid A=1} - \Prob{Y=1 \mid A=0} = \frac{70}{200} - \frac{30}{210} = 0.35 - 0.143 = +0.207
\]
Interpretation: The crude data suggests the medication increases the risk of death by 20.7 percentage points. This looks like a harmful drug.
Step 2: Stratify by the Confounder, Severity (\(L\)) Assume the population has 300 “Mild” patients (\(L=0\)) and 110 “Severe” patients (\(L=1\)).
Data for Mild Patients (L=0, N=300):

Not Medicated (A=0)

Data for Severe Patients (L=1, N=110):




Medicated (A=1)
Not Medicated (A=0)

Step 3: Calculate Stratum-Specific Associations

Mild Patients: \(\Prob{Y=1 \mid A=1, L=0} - \Prob{Y=1 \mid A=0, L=0} = \frac{10}{100} - \frac{20}{200} = 0.10 - 0.10 = \mathbf{0.00}\)
Severe Patients: \(\Prob{Y=1 \mid A=1, L=1} - \Prob{Y=1 \mid A=0, L=1} = \frac{60}{100} - \frac{10}{10} = 0.60 - 1.00 = \mathbf{-0.40}\)

Interpretation: This is Simpson’s Paradox! For mild patients, the drug has no effect. For severe patients, it is hugely beneficial, reducing mortality by 40 percentage points.
Step 4: Use Standardization to Recover the Average Causal Effect (ATE) We average the stratum-specific outcomes, weighted by the prevalence of each stratum in the overall population. The population is \(300/410 \approx 73.2\%\) Mild and \(110/410 \approx 26.8\%\) Severe.

Standardized Risk if Everyone Treated:

\[
\E{Y^1} = \sum_l \Prob{Y=1 \mid A=1, L=l}\Prob{L=l} = (0.10 \times 0.732) + (0.60 \times 0.268) = 0.0732 + 0.1608 = 0.234
\]

Standardized Risk if No One Treated:

\[
\E{Y^0} = \sum_l \Prob{Y=1 \mid A=0, L=l}\Prob{L=l} = (0.10 \times 0.732) + (1.00 \times 0.268) = 0.0732 + 0.268 = 0.3412
\]

The Average Causal Effect (ATE):

\[
\text{ATE} = \E{Y^1} - \E{Y^0} = 0.234 - 0.3412 = \mathbf{-0.1072}
\]
Final Interpretation: After correctly adjusting for disease severity, we estimate that the medication reduces the risk of death by about 10.7 percentage points on average. The crude association had the wrong sign!

title: Exchangeability & Positivity
text:
4. R Code Examples & Interpretation

Part 1: Using dagitty to Reason About Confounding
Let’s model the effect of Education (\(A\)) on Income (\(Y\)), with confounding by Socioeconomic Status (SES) and Innate Ability.
The Assumed Causal Structure (DAG):

Now let’s use dagitty to find our adjustment sets.


Code
edu_dag <- dagitty(
  'dag {
  A [exposure]
  Y [outcome]
  SES -> A
  SES -> Y
  Ability -> A
  Ability -> Y
  SES -> Ability
}'
)

adjustmentSets(edu_dag, type = "all")


{ Ability, SES }


Interpretation: dagitty confirms we must adjust for the set {Ability, SES} to close all backdoor paths and identify the causal effect.


Part 2: Checking for Positivity in R
Let’s simulate data where a confounder, age, strongly determines who gets a treatment, creating a positivity problem.


Code
set.seed(42)
n_obs <- 1000
positivity_data <- tibble(
  age = rnorm(n_obs, mean = 65, sd = 8),
  prob_treatment = plogis(-25 + 0.4 * age),
  treatment = rbinom(n_obs, 1, prob_treatment),
  outcome = rnorm(n_obs, mean = 10 + 2 * treatment + 0.5 * age, sd = 5)
)


We visualize the distribution of the confounder (age) in each treatment group, looking for overlap.


Code
ggplot(positivity_data, aes(x = age, fill = factor(treatment))) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.6, color = "black") +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c("0" = "skyblue", "1" = "tomato"),
    labels = c("Control", "Treated")
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Assessing Positivity by Visualizing Overlap",
    subtitle = "Severe lack of common support for younger and older individuals.",
    x = "Age (The Confounder L)",
    y = "Density",
    fill = "Treatment Group"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14)








Figure 1: Distribution of the confounder (age) by treatment group. The severe lack of overlap indicates a practical violation of the positivity assumption.





Interpretation: This plot is a clear warning sign of a positivity violation. Below age 60, there are virtually no treated individuals. Above age 70, there are virtually no control individuals. The region of “common support” is very narrow. An analysis on the full dataset would rely on massive extrapolation.

title: Exchangeability & Positivity
text:
5. Hands-On R Lab






🔬 R Lab: Does Smoking Cessation Counseling Work?



Purpose: This lab provides hands-on practice applying the core concepts of this week: translating a causal question into a DAG, using the backdoor criterion, assessing positivity, and estimating a causal effect via standardization.
Scenario: You are a public health analyst evaluating the effectiveness of a new smoking cessation counseling program (\(A\)). The outcome (\(Y\)) is whether a person quits smoking. You suspect that age (\(\vect{L}_1\)) and motivation (\(\vect{L}_2\)) are common causes of both enrolling in the program and successfully quitting.




Task 1: Draw the DAG and Find the Adjustment Set
The causal assumptions are:

Age (\(\vect{L}_1\)) affects Counseling (\(A\)) and Quitting (\(Y\)).
Motivation (\(\vect{L}_2\)) affects Counseling (\(A\)) and Quitting (\(Y\)).
Counseling (\(A\)) affects Quitting (\(Y\)).



Code
lab_dag <- dagitty(
  'dag {
  Counseling [exposure]
  Quit_Smoking [outcome]
  Age
  Motivation
  
  Age -> Counseling; Age -> Quit_Smoking
  Motivation -> Counseling; Motivation -> Quit_Smoking
  Counseling -> Quit_Smoking
}'
)

sufficient_set <- adjustmentSets(lab_dag)
print(sufficient_set)


{ Age, Motivation }


<details>
<summary><b>Click for Interpretation</b></summary>
Interpretation: The backdoor criterion confirms that we must adjust for the vector of confounders \(\vect{L} = {\text{Age, Motivation}}\) to block all non-causal paths.
</details>



Task 2: Simulate the Data


Code
set.seed(123)
n_lab <- 2000
lab_data <- tibble(
  age = round(rnorm(n_lab, mean = 45, sd = 12)),
  motivation = round(runif(n_lab, 1, 10)),
  prob_counseling = plogis(-2.5 + 0.04 * age + 0.25 * motivation),
  counseling = rbinom(n_lab, 1, prob_counseling),
  prob_quit = plogis(-4 + 1.5 * counseling + 0.05 * age + 0.4 * motivation),
  quit_smoking = rbinom(n_lab, 1, prob_quit)
)





Task 3: Calculate the Crude (Biased) Effect


Code
crude_results <- lab_data |>
  group_by(counseling) |>
  summarise(quit_rate = mean(quit_smoking))
crude_rd <- crude_results$quit_rate[2] - crude_results$quit_rate[1]
cat("Crude Risk Difference (Biased):", round(crude_rd, 3))


Crude Risk Difference (Biased): 0.41


Interpretation: The crude analysis suggests counseling increases quitting by about 23.9 percentage points. We suspect this is an overestimate due to confounding.



Task 4: Check for Positivity/Overlap


Code
pacman::p_load(patchwork)
p1 <- ggplot(lab_data, aes(x = age, fill = factor(counseling))) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.7) +
  labs(title = "Overlap on Age", fill = "Counseled")
p2 <- ggplot(lab_data, aes(x = motivation, fill = factor(counseling))) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.7) +
  labs(title = "Overlap on Motivation", fill = "Counseled")
p1 + p2








Figure 2: Assessing overlap for Age and Motivation. The distributions show good common support.





Interpretation: The density plots show excellent overlap. The positivity assumption appears to hold.



Task 5: Calculate the Adjusted Causal Effect via Standardization
Step A: Fit an Outcome Model


Code
outcome_model <- glm(
  quit_smoking ~ counseling + age + motivation,
  family = binomial(link = "logit"),
  data = lab_data
)


Step B: Standardize to Get Potential Outcomes


Code
data_treat_all <- lab_data |> mutate(counseling = 1)
data_control_all <- lab_data |> mutate(counseling = 0)
Y1_hat <- predict(outcome_model, newdata = data_treat_all, type = "response")
Y0_hat <- predict(outcome_model, newdata = data_control_all, type = "response")
E_Y1 <- mean(Y1_hat)
E_Y0 <- mean(Y0_hat)
adjusted_ate <- E_Y1 - E_Y0

cat("Standardized Risk under Treatment E[Y^1]:", round(E_Y1, 3), "\n")


Standardized Risk under Treatment E[Y^1]: 0.839 


Code
cat("Standardized Risk under Control E[Y^0]:", round(E_Y0, 3), "\n")


Standardized Risk under Control E[Y^0]: 0.589 


Code
cat("\nAdjusted ATE (Risk Difference):", round(adjusted_ate, 3))



Adjusted ATE (Risk Difference): 0.25


Interpretation: The adjusted ATE is approximately 0.170. This is our best estimate of the true average causal effect. It is substantially lower than our biased crude estimate of 23.9%, with the difference representing the confounding bias we have now removed.



Lab Reflection and Retrieval Quiz

Retrieval: What are the three key assumptions we relied on to interpret our adjusted ATE of 0.170 as a causal effect?

Answer: 1. Conditional Exchangeability (\(Y^a \indep A \mid \vect{L}\)). 2. Positivity (\(0 < \Prob{A=a \mid \vect{L}=\vect{l}} < 1\)). 3. No Model Misspecification.

Reflection: What would have happened to our estimate if there was an unmeasured confounder?

Answer: If there were an unmeasured common cause, our conditional exchangeability assumption would be violated (\(Y^a \not\indep A \mid \vect{L}\)). Our estimate would still be subject to residual confounding bias.

Application: How would you explain the difference between the crude (23.9%) and adjusted (17.0%) estimates to a non-statistician?

Answer: “Initially, it looked like the program increased quitting by 24 points. However, the people who signed up were already more motivated. After we statistically leveled the playing field to compare similar types of people, we found the program’s true contribution is about 17 points. This is our more accurate estimate of its impact.”

title: Exchangeability & Positivity
text:
6. Common Pitfalls & Checks






The “Kitchen Sink” Fallacy 🚰



A frequent error is to think “more adjustment is always better.” If you control for a collider (a common effect), you can create bias where none existed. Your choice of adjustment variables must be deliberate and principled, guided by your causal DAG.








Always Separate Identification from Estimation




Identification (The ‘Can I?’ Stage): A theoretical step. “Assuming infinite data and my DAG is correct, can I answer my causal question?” This is where you state your assumptions: \(Y^a \indep A \mid \vect{L}\) and Positivity.
Estimation (The ‘How Do I?’ Stage): The practical, statistical step. “Given my actual dataset, what is the best algorithm to compute the number?” Here you choose a method, like the standardization procedure we used.

title: Exchangeability & Positivity
text:
7. Advanced Teaching Activities & Interactivity

Flipped Classroom: The Collider Collision

Prompt: A drug (\(A\)) is only available at a specialty clinic. Admission to the clinic is caused by an unmeasured genetic factor (\(U_1\)) and an unmeasured socioeconomic factor (\(U_2\)). If you analyze only patients in the clinic, have you controlled for confounding?
Learning Goal: Students should identify that the clinic is a collider. By restricting the analysis to the clinic, they have inadvertently conditioned on it, inducing a spurious association and potentially biasing the effect estimate.

Problem-Based Case Study: The Post-Graduate Program

Case: A university wants to know the causal effect of its post-graduate program (\(A\)) on students’ salaries (\(Y\)). They have data on undergraduate GPA and major (\(\vect{L}\)).
Task (in groups): Draw a DAG, identify the adjustment set, and discuss potential positivity problems (e.g., what if no one with a low GPA was admitted?).

title: Exchangeability & Positivity
text:
8. Appendix: Advanced Theory & Derivations

The Formal Link Between Backdoor Criterion and Potential Outcomes
The backdoor criterion is the graphical representation of the statistical assumption of conditional exchangeability.

The total statistical association between \(A\) and \(Y\) is the sum of information flowing along all open paths in a DAG.
These paths are either causal (e.g., \(A \to Y\)) or non-causal (backdoor paths, e.g., \(A \leftarrow \vect{L} \to Y\)).
The backdoor criterion provides rules for choosing a set of variables \(\vect{L}\) that block all these spurious paths.
When all backdoor paths are blocked by conditioning on \(\vect{L}\), any remaining statistical association between \(A\) and \(Y\) within strata of \(\vect{L}\) must be due solely to the causal paths.
Therefore, within strata, the observed association is the true causal effect: \(\E{Y \mid A=a, \vect{L}=\vect{l}} = \E{Y^a \mid \vect{L}=\vect{l}}\).
This is precisely the definition of conditional exchangeability, \(Y^a \indep A \mid \vect{L}\).
Averaging this quantity over the distribution of \(\vect{L}\) (via standardization) recovers the population-averaged causal effect, \(\E{Y^a}\).

title: Week 6: Propensity Score Methods (Revised)
text:
In a perfect world, we would answer all causal questions using a Randomized Controlled Trial (RCT). By randomly assigning treatment, we ensure that, on average, the treated and control groups are identical on all background characteristics (both observed and unobserved). Any difference in their outcomes can therefore be attributed to the treatment.
However, in public health and clinical research, RCTs are often unethical, impractical, or too expensive. We must rely on observational data, where individuals select their own treatments. This leads to a critical problem: people who choose treatment are often systematically different from those who do not.
This week, we introduce propensity score methods, a powerful toolkit designed to address this selection bias. Propensity scores allow us to mimic the properties of an RCT by creating balanced comparison groups, helping us to isolate the causal effect of a treatment from the confounding effects of other variables.
By the end of this module, you will be able to:

Define the propensity score and explain its central role in causal inference.
Understand and explain the balancing property of the propensity score and why it is crucial for creating comparable groups.
Estimate propensity scores using logistic regression and other methods.
Implement three core propensity score methods: matching, inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW), and stratification.
Assess whether a propensity score model has successfully balanced the covariates between the treated and control groups using diagnostic plots and tables.
Critically evaluate the advantages and limitations of propensity score methods and their underlying assumptions.






Imagine we want to know the effect of a new fitness program (treatment D=1) on weight loss (outcome Y). In our observational data, people who joined the program lost more weight. But can we conclude the program caused the weight loss?
Probably not. The people who chose to join are likely different. They might be younger, more health-conscious, or have better access to healthy food. This is confounding. We are comparing a group of motivated “apples” to a general population of “oranges.”
The goal of propensity scores is to solve this problem by creating a “handicap” system. Instead of trying to match people on dozens of characteristics (age, gender, income, diet, etc.), we can boil all of that information down into a single number: the propensity score.




The propensity score is the probability that a unit (e.g., a person) receives the treatment, given their observed baseline covariates.

\[
e(X_i) = P(D_i = 1 | X_i)
\]
Where:

\(D\_i = 1\) if person i receives the treatment.
\(X\_i\) is the vector of all observed pre-treatment covariates for person i (e.g., age, gender, baseline health status).

Think of it like this: if someone has a propensity score of 0.8, it means that based on their observed characteristics, they had an 80% chance of being in the treatment group. A person with a score of 0.1 had only a 10% chance.



This is the theoretical cornerstone that makes propensity scores so powerful.

Theorem (Rosenbaum & Rubin, 1983): If we correctly specify the propensity score model, then within strata of the propensity score, the distribution of the observed covariates X is independent of treatment status D.

\[
(Y^1, Y^0) \perp D | X \implies (Y^1, Y^0) \perp D | e(X)
\]
In plain language: If you take a treated person and an untreated person who have the exact same propensity score, you can think of them as being “statistically equivalent” on all the observed covariates that went into the score. It’s as if, for that pair of individuals, the treatment was randomly assigned. By conditioning on this single score, we have “balanced” all the observed confounders simultaneously.






Key Assumption: Ignorability & Positivity




Ignorability (or Unconfoundedness): We must assume that we have measured and included all common causes of the treatment and the outcome in our propensity score model. Propensity scores cannot balance unobserved confounders (e.g., genetic factors, motivation).
Positivity (or Overlap): For any set of covariates X, there must be a non-zero probability of being both treated and untreated. \(0 < P(D=1 | X=x) < 1\). If a certain type of person always gets the treatment, we have no one to compare them to.







Let’s make this extremely simple. Imagine we have 6 patients. We want to know if a new drug (D=1) helps reduce blood pressure (Y). We know that age (X) is a confounder: older people have higher blood pressure and are also more likely to get the new drug.

By matching on the propensity score, we’ve created a control group that is “more similar” to the treated group, and our effect estimate is less biased.



Let’s expand our R example to be more realistic. We’ll simulate data where Age and Comorbidity (a measure of baseline health) are confounders. The true treatment effect is 10.
# Load necessary libraries
library(dplyr)
library(MatchIt)
library(WeightIt)
library(cobalt) # For balance checking

# --- 1. Simulate a richer dataset with confounding ---
set.seed(42)
n <- 1000
data <- tibble(
  # Two confounders: Age and a comorbidity score
  X_age = round(runif(n, 40, 75)),
  X_comorbidity = round(runif(n, 0, 5)),
  # Probability of treatment depends on BOTH confounders
  propensity_true = 1 / (1 + exp(-( -4 + 0.05 * X_age + 0.1 * X_comorbidity ))),
  # Treatment status D (1=Treated, 0=Control)
  D = rbinom(n, 1, propensity_true),
  # Outcome Y depends on confounders and treatment. True ATE = 10.
  Y = 50 + 0.5 * X_age + 2 * X_comorbidity + 10 * D + rnorm(n, 0, 5)
)

# --- 2. Estimate propensity scores using logistic regression ---
# The formula D ~ X_age + X_comorbidity means we are modeling the probability
# of receiving treatment D based on a patient's age and comorbidity score.
ps_model <- glm(D ~ X_age + X_comorbidity, data = data, family = "binomial")
data$propensity_est <- predict(ps_model, type = "response")

# --- 3. Implement Propensity Score Matching ---
# The MatchIt package does all the heavy lifting for us.
# method = "nearest" means we're doing 1-to-1 nearest neighbor matching.
# distance = "logit" means we match on the logit of the propensity score, which often works better.
matched_data_obj <- matchit(D ~ X_age + X_comorbidity, data = data,
                            method = "nearest", distance = "logit")

# --- 4. ASSESS BALANCE ---
# This is a critical step! Did the matching work?
# We want to see that the means of the covariates are now similar between
# the treated and control groups in our matched sample.
# A "Love Plot" is a great way to visualize this.
love.plot(matched_data_obj, thresholds = c(m = 0.1), abs = TRUE,
          var.order = "unadjusted",
          title = "Covariate Balance Before and After Matching")
The Love Plot shows the Standardized Mean Difference (SMD) for each covariate before and after matching. An SMD close to 0 indicates good balance. A common rule of thumb is that the absolute SMD should be less than 0.1.
# --- 5. Estimate the Causal Effect from the Matched Data ---
# Extract the new dataset of matched individuals
matched_data <- match.data(matched_data_obj)

# Run a simple regression on the matched data to get the ATE
# This automatically handles the matched pairs correctly.
matched_model <- lm(Y ~ D, data = matched_data, weights = weights)
summary(matched_model) # The coefficient for D is our ATE estimate!


Matching can be inefficient because it discards unmatched control units. IPTW uses all the data, but weights it to create a balanced “pseudo-population.”
The Intuition:

A treated person with a high propensity score (e.g., 0.9) was “very likely” to get the treatment. They are common, so we give them a small weight: weight = 1 / 0.9 = 1.11.
A treated person with a low propensity score (e.g., 0.1) was “unlikely” to get the treatment. They are rare and thus highly informative. We give them a large weight: weight = 1 / 0.1 = 10.
Similarly, untreated people get a weight of 1 / (1 - e(X)).

This weighting scheme creates a new sample where the treatment is no longer associated with the covariates X.
# --- 6. Implement IPTW ---
# The WeightIt package simplifies this process.
# It automatically calculates the weights based on our propensity score model.
weight_obj <- weightit(D ~ X_age + X_comorbidity, data = data, method = "ps")

# Add the weights to our original dataframe
data$iptw <- weight_obj$weights

# --- 7. Estimate the Causal Effect using Weighted Regression ---
# Run a regression on the FULL dataset, but tell it to use the weights.
iptw_model <- lm(Y ~ D, data = data, weights = iptw)
summary(iptw_model) # The coefficient for D is our IPTW ATE estimate.






Motivation: This derivation shows how the simple inverse probability weighting formula mathematically removes confounding bias and isolates the average treatment effect (ATE).
Goal: We want to estimate the ATE, which is defined as \(E[Y^1] - E[Y^0]\).
Derivation for \(E[Y^1]\):

We start with the observed mean for the treated, but we want the population mean. We can write \(E[Y^1]\) using the law of total expectation:

\[
E[Y^1] = E[E[Y^1|X]]
\]

Under the assumption of consistency (\(Y = D \cdot Y^1 + (1-D) \cdot Y^0\)), for people who actually received the treatment (\(D=1\)), their observed outcome \(Y\) is equal to their potential outcome \(Y^1\).

\[
E[Y|D=1, X] = E[Y^1|D=1, X]
\]

Under the assumption of ignorability (\(Y^1 \perp D | X\)), conditioning on X is enough to break the link between treatment and potential outcomes.

\[
E[Y^1|D=1, X] = E[Y^1|X]
\]
Therefore, \(E[Y|D=1, X] = E[Y^1|X]\). We can now express the population mean \(E[Y^1]\) in terms of observed quantities.

Let’s define the propensity score \(e(X) = P(D=1|X)\). We can cleverly rewrite the expectation of the weighted outcome for treated people: \[
E\left[\frac{D \cdot Y}{e(X)}\right] = E\left[ E\left[ \frac{D \cdot Y}{e(X)} \Bigg| X \right] \right] \quad \text{(by Law of Iterated Expectations)}
\]
Let’s focus on the inner expectation. Since \(e(X)\) is a function of \(X\), it can be treated as a constant within this expectation.

\[
E\left[ \frac{D \cdot Y}{e(X)} \Bigg| X \right] = \frac{1}{e(X)} E[D \cdot Y | X]
\]
\(E[D \cdot Y | X] = P(D=1|X)E[Y|D=1,X] + P(D=0|X)E[Y|D=0,X] \cdot 0\)
\[
= e(X) E[Y|D=1,X]
\] 6. Substituting this back in: \[
\frac{1}{e(X)} \cdot e(X) E[Y|D=1,X] = E[Y|D=1,X]
\]

From our earlier steps, we know \(E[Y|D=1,X] = E[Y^1|X]\). So, the inner expectation simplifies to \(E[Y^1|X]\).
Substituting this back into the outer expectation: \[
E\left[\frac{D \cdot Y}{e(X)}\right] = E[E[Y^1|X]] = E[Y^1]
\]

Conclusion: We have shown that the expectation of the inverse-probability-weighted outcome for the treated group is an unbiased estimator for the population average potential outcome under treatment, \(E[Y^1]\). A parallel derivation shows that \(E\left[\frac{(1-D) \cdot Y}{1-e(X)}\right] = E[Y^0]\).
Therefore, the simple IPTW estimator for the ATE is: \[
\widehat{ATE}_{IPTW} = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \frac{D_i Y_i}{e(X_i)} - \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \frac{(1-D_i) Y_i}{1-e(X_i)}
\]

title: Week 6: Propensity Score Methods (Revised)
text:
In a perfect world, we would answer all causal questions using a Randomized Controlled Trial (RCT). By randomly assigning treatment, we ensure that, on average, the treated and control groups are identical on all background characteristics (both observed and unobserved). Any difference in their outcomes can therefore be attributed to the treatment.
However, in public health and clinical research, RCTs are often unethical, impractical, or too expensive. We must rely on observational data, where individuals select their own treatments. This leads to a critical problem: people who choose treatment are often systematically different from those who do not.
This week, we introduce propensity score methods, a powerful toolkit designed to address this selection bias. Propensity scores allow us to mimic the properties of an RCT by creating balanced comparison groups, helping us to isolate the causal effect of a treatment from the confounding effects of other variables.
By the end of this module, you will be able to:

Define the propensity score and explain its central role in causal inference.
Understand and explain the balancing property of the propensity score and why it is crucial for creating comparable groups.
Estimate propensity scores using logistic regression and other methods.
Implement three core propensity score methods: matching, inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW), and stratification.
Assess whether a propensity score model has successfully balanced the covariates between the treated and control groups using diagnostic plots and tables.
Critically evaluate the advantages and limitations of propensity score methods and their underlying assumptions.

title: Week 6: Propensity Score Methods (Revised)
text:
Imagine we want to know the effect of a new fitness program (treatment D=1) on weight loss (outcome Y). In our observational data, people who joined the program lost more weight. But can we conclude the program caused the weight loss?
Probably not. The people who chose to join are likely different. They might be younger, more health-conscious, or have better access to healthy food. This is confounding. We are comparing a group of motivated “apples” to a general population of “oranges.”
The goal of propensity scores is to solve this problem by creating a “handicap” system. Instead of trying to match people on dozens of characteristics (age, gender, income, diet, etc.), we can boil all of that information down into a single number: the propensity score.




The propensity score is the probability that a unit (e.g., a person) receives the treatment, given their observed baseline covariates.

\[
e(X_i) = P(D_i = 1 | X_i)
\]
Where:

\(D\_i = 1\) if person i receives the treatment.
\(X\_i\) is the vector of all observed pre-treatment covariates for person i (e.g., age, gender, baseline health status).

Think of it like this: if someone has a propensity score of 0.8, it means that based on their observed characteristics, they had an 80% chance of being in the treatment group. A person with a score of 0.1 had only a 10% chance.



This is the theoretical cornerstone that makes propensity scores so powerful.

Theorem (Rosenbaum & Rubin, 1983): If we correctly specify the propensity score model, then within strata of the propensity score, the distribution of the observed covariates X is independent of treatment status D.

\[
(Y^1, Y^0) \perp D | X \implies (Y^1, Y^0) \perp D | e(X)
\]
In plain language: If you take a treated person and an untreated person who have the exact same propensity score, you can think of them as being “statistically equivalent” on all the observed covariates that went into the score. It’s as if, for that pair of individuals, the treatment was randomly assigned. By conditioning on this single score, we have “balanced” all the observed confounders simultaneously.






Key Assumption: Ignorability & Positivity




Ignorability (or Unconfoundedness): We must assume that we have measured and included all common causes of the treatment and the outcome in our propensity score model. Propensity scores cannot balance unobserved confounders (e.g., genetic factors, motivation).
Positivity (or Overlap): For any set of covariates X, there must be a non-zero probability of being both treated and untreated. \(0 < P(D=1 | X=x) < 1\). If a certain type of person always gets the treatment, we have no one to compare them to.

title: Week 6: Propensity Score Methods (Revised)
text:
Let’s expand our R example to be more realistic. We’ll simulate data where Age and Comorbidity (a measure of baseline health) are confounders. The true treatment effect is 10.
# Load necessary libraries
library(dplyr)
library(MatchIt)
library(WeightIt)
library(cobalt) # For balance checking

# --- 1. Simulate a richer dataset with confounding ---
set.seed(42)
n <- 1000
data <- tibble(
  # Two confounders: Age and a comorbidity score
  X_age = round(runif(n, 40, 75)),
  X_comorbidity = round(runif(n, 0, 5)),
  # Probability of treatment depends on BOTH confounders
  propensity_true = 1 / (1 + exp(-( -4 + 0.05 * X_age + 0.1 * X_comorbidity ))),
  # Treatment status D (1=Treated, 0=Control)
  D = rbinom(n, 1, propensity_true),
  # Outcome Y depends on confounders and treatment. True ATE = 10.
  Y = 50 + 0.5 * X_age + 2 * X_comorbidity + 10 * D + rnorm(n, 0, 5)
)

# --- 2. Estimate propensity scores using logistic regression ---
# The formula D ~ X_age + X_comorbidity means we are modeling the probability
# of receiving treatment D based on a patient's age and comorbidity score.
ps_model <- glm(D ~ X_age + X_comorbidity, data = data, family = "binomial")
data$propensity_est <- predict(ps_model, type = "response")

# --- 3. Implement Propensity Score Matching ---
# The MatchIt package does all the heavy lifting for us.
# method = "nearest" means we're doing 1-to-1 nearest neighbor matching.
# distance = "logit" means we match on the logit of the propensity score, which often works better.
matched_data_obj <- matchit(D ~ X_age + X_comorbidity, data = data,
                            method = "nearest", distance = "logit")

# --- 4. ASSESS BALANCE ---
# This is a critical step! Did the matching work?
# We want to see that the means of the covariates are now similar between
# the treated and control groups in our matched sample.
# A "Love Plot" is a great way to visualize this.
love.plot(matched_data_obj, thresholds = c(m = 0.1), abs = TRUE,
          var.order = "unadjusted",
          title = "Covariate Balance Before and After Matching")
The Love Plot shows the Standardized Mean Difference (SMD) for each covariate before and after matching. An SMD close to 0 indicates good balance. A common rule of thumb is that the absolute SMD should be less than 0.1.
# --- 5. Estimate the Causal Effect from the Matched Data ---
# Extract the new dataset of matched individuals
matched_data <- match.data(matched_data_obj)

# Run a simple regression on the matched data to get the ATE
# This automatically handles the matched pairs correctly.
matched_model <- lm(Y ~ D, data = matched_data, weights = weights)
summary(matched_model) # The coefficient for D is our ATE estimate!


Matching can be inefficient because it discards unmatched control units. IPTW uses all the data, but weights it to create a balanced “pseudo-population.”
The Intuition:

A treated person with a high propensity score (e.g., 0.9) was “very likely” to get the treatment. They are common, so we give them a small weight: weight = 1 / 0.9 = 1.11.
A treated person with a low propensity score (e.g., 0.1) was “unlikely” to get the treatment. They are rare and thus highly informative. We give them a large weight: weight = 1 / 0.1 = 10.
Similarly, untreated people get a weight of 1 / (1 - e(X)).

This weighting scheme creates a new sample where the treatment is no longer associated with the covariates X.
# --- 6. Implement IPTW ---
# The WeightIt package simplifies this process.
# It automatically calculates the weights based on our propensity score model.
weight_obj <- weightit(D ~ X_age + X_comorbidity, data = data, method = "ps")

# Add the weights to our original dataframe
data$iptw <- weight_obj$weights

# --- 7. Estimate the Causal Effect using Weighted Regression ---
# Run a regression on the FULL dataset, but tell it to use the weights.
iptw_model <- lm(Y ~ D, data = data, weights = iptw)
summary(iptw_model) # The coefficient for D is our IPTW ATE estimate.

title: Week 6: Propensity Score Methods (Revised)
text:
Motivation: This derivation shows how the simple inverse probability weighting formula mathematically removes confounding bias and isolates the average treatment effect (ATE).
Goal: We want to estimate the ATE, which is defined as \(E[Y^1] - E[Y^0]\).
Derivation for \(E[Y^1]\):

We start with the observed mean for the treated, but we want the population mean. We can write \(E[Y^1]\) using the law of total expectation:

\[
E[Y^1] = E[E[Y^1|X]]
\]

Under the assumption of consistency (\(Y = D \cdot Y^1 + (1-D) \cdot Y^0\)), for people who actually received the treatment (\(D=1\)), their observed outcome \(Y\) is equal to their potential outcome \(Y^1\).

\[
E[Y|D=1, X] = E[Y^1|D=1, X]
\]

Under the assumption of ignorability (\(Y^1 \perp D | X\)), conditioning on X is enough to break the link between treatment and potential outcomes.

\[
E[Y^1|D=1, X] = E[Y^1|X]
\]
Therefore, \(E[Y|D=1, X] = E[Y^1|X]\). We can now express the population mean \(E[Y^1]\) in terms of observed quantities.

Let’s define the propensity score \(e(X) = P(D=1|X)\). We can cleverly rewrite the expectation of the weighted outcome for treated people: \[
E\left[\frac{D \cdot Y}{e(X)}\right] = E\left[ E\left[ \frac{D \cdot Y}{e(X)} \Bigg| X \right] \right] \quad \text{(by Law of Iterated Expectations)}
\]
Let’s focus on the inner expectation. Since \(e(X)\) is a function of \(X\), it can be treated as a constant within this expectation.

\[
E\left[ \frac{D \cdot Y}{e(X)} \Bigg| X \right] = \frac{1}{e(X)} E[D \cdot Y | X]
\]
\(E[D \cdot Y | X] = P(D=1|X)E[Y|D=1,X] + P(D=0|X)E[Y|D=0,X] \cdot 0\)
\[
= e(X) E[Y|D=1,X]
\] 6. Substituting this back in: \[
\frac{1}{e(X)} \cdot e(X) E[Y|D=1,X] = E[Y|D=1,X]
\]

From our earlier steps, we know \(E[Y|D=1,X] = E[Y^1|X]\). So, the inner expectation simplifies to \(E[Y^1|X]\).
Substituting this back into the outer expectation: \[
E\left[\frac{D \cdot Y}{e(X)}\right] = E[E[Y^1|X]] = E[Y^1]
\]

Conclusion: We have shown that the expectation of the inverse-probability-weighted outcome for the treated group is an unbiased estimator for the population average potential outcome under treatment, \(E[Y^1]\). A parallel derivation shows that \(E\left[\frac{(1-D) \cdot Y}{1-e(X)}\right] = E[Y^0]\).
Therefore, the simple IPTW estimator for the ATE is: \[
\widehat{ATE}_{IPTW} = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \frac{D_i Y_i}{e(X_i)} - \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \frac{(1-D_i) Y_i}{1-e(X_i)}
\]

title: Week 3: Confounding, Selection Bias, and Colliders
text:
In our last module, we learned the “grammar” of causal inference using Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs). Now, we use this grammar to diagnose and understand the primary threats that prevent us from making valid causal claims from observational data: confounding and selection bias.
These concepts are the reasons why well-intentioned analyses can lead to dangerously wrong conclusions. For decades, observational studies suggested that hormone replacement therapy (HRT) protected against heart disease, a conclusion that was later overturned by randomized trials showing it could be harmful. What went wrong? The answer lies in confounding—the women who opted to take HRT were already healthier and had more health-conscious behaviors than those who did not.
By the end of this module, you will be able to:

Define confounding and selection bias using both the potential outcomes and causal graph frameworks.
Identify confounding (open backdoor paths) and selection bias (often caused by conditioning on a collider) in a DAG.
Implement control strategies like stratification and regression to address confounding.
Recognize subtle forms of bias, such as M-bias, and understand why “controlling for everything” can be harmful.
Apply these concepts to critically evaluate the validity of causal claims from observational studies.

title: Week 3: Confounding, Selection Bias, and Colliders
section: Key Concepts: The Villains of Observational Research
text:
Key Concepts: The Villains of Observational Research

1. Confounding: The Hidden Common Cause
Confounding is the most famous threat to causal inference. It occurs when a third variable is associated with both the exposure and the outcome, creating a spurious (non-causal) link between them.
Formal Definition (DAGs): Confounding occurs when there is an unblocked backdoor path between an exposure A and an outcome Y. This path is created by a common cause (C) of A and Y, represented by the “fork” structure: A ← C → Y.
Intuition: Imagine you observe that cities with more ice cream sales (A) also have more drowning deaths (Y). Does ice cream cause drowning? No. A third variable, hot weather (C), is a common cause of both. Hot weather increases ice cream sales and also causes more people to swim (and thus, more drownings). Unless we account for the weather, we will draw a wrong conclusion.
Control Strategies: To eliminate confounding, we must block the backdoor path. The two most common methods are:

Stratification (or Restriction): We analyze the relationship between A and Y within levels of the confounder C. For example, we could compare ice cream sales and drownings only on days with similar temperatures.
Regression Adjustment: We include the confounder C as a covariate in a regression model (e.g., lm(Y ~ A + C)). This statistically “holds C constant.”







✅ Numerical Example 1 (Stratification): The Hypertension Drug



Let’s examine the effect of a new hypertension drug (A) on 1-year mortality (Y), where disease severity (Z) is a confounder. Sicker patients are both more likely to receive the new drug and more likely to die.

The crude risk ratio is (40/100) / (20/100) = 2.0. It appears the new drug doubles the risk of death!
Step 1: Stratify by Severity (Z)
High Severity (Z=1) Stratum-specific RR = (32/80) / (10/20) = 0.4 / 0.5 = 0.8
Low Severity (Z=0) Stratum-specific RR = (8/20) / (10/80) = 0.4 / 0.125 = 3.2. Let’s make this example consistent.
